review:
Very interesting space sandbox marred by a wonky interface and stability issues.

VD2 is a space sandbox game where you start from near-nothing and work your way up to ruling the entire sector with an iron fist. It has some features I haven't seen in any other sandbox games which I think are really cool, such as missions which restrict ship usage or fleet size so that you can't just steamroll a tough mission by grinding for an hour and then showing up with a massive fleet. The game also uses a reserve system which has only a portion of your fleet showing up for any battle (mission or otherwise), which serves the dual purposes of keeping the endgame challenging and keeping your PC from melting.

Not that you want to have too massive a fleet, because the game tends to get a bit crashy, especially at scale.

You immediately have to decide whether you're playing story mode or sandbox mode. Given my experience with other space sandbox games this felt like a weird choice, but after completing the story mode I understood why the dichotomy: in most sandbox games, completing the story leaves the sandbox open to you, while completing the VD2 story leaves the game's world completely broken. The story is interesting, and it's a real shame the endgame is so unsatisfying. 

Also, while trying to avoid major spoilers, the endgame also gets tedious. The ships you have to fight spawn CONSTANTLY and even with a fleet full of capital ships take so much of a pounding that you're going to spend 20 minutes on a single battle. Not a major fight that's the culmination of maneuvering and strategy...just one fight in a series of endless battles just to keep from losing ground.

The interface is also extremely weird and almost caused me to quit a couple of hours in. Now, most space sandbox games require you to contend with a menu salad that, by the end of the game, feels more like you're playing an Excel simulator than flying a spaceship, so I'm grading on a curve here. But even by the standards of the genre, VD2's interface is clunky and idiosyncratic and it's weirdly hard to do certain things that should be very normal.

There are several cool things that make this game very unique among space sandbox games. If this were early access, I'd say buy it, support the developer, and the bugs and wonky bits will get ironed out before release. As this is a mature title not seeing updates anymore, I think you should only bite if you're willing to fight with the game a bit to experience all the good parts that this quirky, unique title has to offer.

This game is VERY ambitious for a single man to develop, and it shows in places.  It can crash every couple of hours when it compiles too much script, and it can bug out a bit with clipping in large battles, pretty standard stuff, and it has frequent auto-saves to compensate. But that's also the good part. This game asks "What if you could play Homeworld, the GOOD version, both as fleet command and an individual pilot?" 

The first one tried to do the same and set up a compelling story.  But it was very difficult to learn the interface, as one might expect. This one is easier, doesn't have such punishing graphics, allowing for larger fleet battles, but you're also in charge of a lot more. Automatic resource trading (money printer) and a Remote Interface permit you to take charge of multiple fleets in turn, across an entire theater of the Oort Cloud. 

It's amazing one you get the hang of things. You really will feel like your player character is supposed to feel. You are a Stub. A person who sold their body, their memories, and their former life for some unknown reason. You play and find what yuo want to be. SPOILERS FROM HERE ON IN. DO NOT READ EXCEPT FOR CONTEXT IF YOU'RE CONFUSED. 
-------------------------------------------------------------



You are going to LOSE this game. It's advanced alien invasions done right. NO matter how good you are, no matter how efficient, you will lose in the end. You have to crawl past impossible odds, likely learning over and over again how to set up anything resembling a resistance.  You cannot win, only delay. 

So why do that? To set up the sequel and provide a fun environment for players to learn this punishing game. It even lets you legally cheat, to gentle the learning curve, and it remains challenging. You can't even do fairly well by thinking like a casual, or if space RTS combat isn't something you want to invest time in. You are Fleet Command, dared to make use of your advanced cognitive capabilities in order to forestall the threat. Not just planning, but pre-planning, hardcore, because you are going to get your ass kicked until you don't. 

And when you finally figure out YOUR best ways to avoid total destruction, it a rewarding experience. Just the lore from this game as a standalone, however seemingly sparse, can fuel your imagination for years. What would you do as a Stub? If everything you think you are is gone, what would you choose to be?

I like what the game was aiming for, and it seems to have been made by a dedicated team. It is sort of a more chill/lite version of X4.
However, there are some serious issues with the game that mean that I cannot recommend it. If they could be fixed, then the game would be decent.
The game has serious instability. Luckily autosaves are frequent, so you usually don't lose much progress. But when it crashes at the end of a big fight that may have taken over 30 minutes that is very frustrating. The "tactical" screen is abysmal, it has zooming, panning/rotating and sensitivity issues. Homeworld 1 figured out how handle commanding units in 3D 25years ago, so I'm not sure why devs struggle to replicate it. The automatic fleet combat is core to the endgame, but the calculations are not explained, so getting fleet composition correct is a guessing game.

No, this is a bad, broken game. I regret the time I have wasted learning, and playing, and more than anything, suffering through it.

1. Crashing. This game crashes, a lot. At first, it doesn't seem that bad, a crash every hour or two at most. With the autosaving that sets things back no more than 5 minutes, as missions and battles are short. But get farther in where you have maxed fleets, and crashes happen constantly,  every other battle. These battles are long, and cleaning up fighters can often be a grind, then having the game crash to do it all over again. Or 20-30 minutes of tedious fleet and base management. Infuriating.

2. UI. What a mess, and an unintuitive one at that. Who thinks hotkeys like Shift+C to open coms to request docking with station is a good idea? But the issues go far beyond hotkeys. The UI is poorly designed, so selecting and moving ships, managing bases and fleets, setting up trade and mining, it all a huge pain to do. Even just finding where ships are in a battle is a challenge, as you get either massive icons covering up all the ships, or no icons and you have to find the dark smudge in the background...

3. Difficulty/scripting. So let me tell you a story, you take some missions from a station, they want you to go do some thing, and you fight a few pirate fighters. You manage to win, and get some credits, which allow you to upgrade your ship so you can win easier. Now you look at the next higher paying mission, defend the station from some pirates. It pays a bit more, so it's probably a bit harder, but you should be ready for it, right? How about no, it's borderline impossible, needing either an endgame fleet, or far higher tier of ship and upgrades to even stand a chance...

This is the norm, for the entire game. Every story mission is a roll of the dice of being normal, boring, or absurdly impossible. It isn't a matter of coming back with better ships, the dev didn't want players to do that, so you are limited in how many and what kind you can bring, for some reason... Some missions are just strait up impossible, unless you use some tedious cheese strat. Talon in particular stands out, as the game wants you to fight an endgame super enemy, with a small force early in the game.

4. Overworld diplomacy and endgame enemy faction. Both of these, are incredibly unfun and tedious to deal with. Try and do anything clever, and the strongest faction starts a total war with you. Spend half an hour setting up trade ships and escorts, then they die and need to be rebuilt because a doomstack just happened to target them despite the trade ships having the highest level cloaking. Try to set up a supply for a base, well it takes time to commision and build the trade ship, then time to build the resource ship, then you have to position it to build away from other buildings, but also POIs that don't properly show their ring of influence, then you have to scroll through a list of 100 ships to set up the trade ship to have make use of it. Then after all that some enemy comes by and kills it all so you have to do it all again. Oh yea, and some of this can only be done inside a base, not even the same base, other parts need to be done outside a base.

Now for the endgame enemy faction, they are not fun to fight. High damage, very tanky, immune to capture, immune to abilities, barriers block most weapons, can disable your ship for 90% of the battle, and pull your ships into their deathball from across the map, and they have hitscan weapons so no dodging allowed, or counterplay to any of these things! On the overworld they spawn massive fleets stronger than the player can make, faster than the player can, and don't have a base to attack or any way to fight back.

Once they show up, nothing else in the overworld matters. They steamroll everything, your trade ships, your bases, and the other factions as well. No point in wasting time building anything, going to war to expand just accelerates their steamrolling of the map. 

5. A 1 dev project. This game has a lot of ambition, fleets of ships ranging from fighter, up to capital ships. Battles have countless projectiles, missiles, and independantly targetting turrets. There are abilities, upgrades, fleet formations, reserve ships, commands, etc. Then there is the overworld, several different factions, with completely different ships, behaviors, trade and structures that the player can influence, build, and conquer. There is just so much, and that's the issue. It's too much for most small teams, let alone a single person to make and implement in a polished and coherent game. 

I don't want to finish the game, it's no longer fun. Thankfully I can't, I ran into a mission I don't know how to cheese. It spawns me 50km from the starting point, so a 10 minute journey just to start. Then the battle starts, where I have to protect a ship, that at one point has a bunch of enemies spawn on top of them. If a single one happens to target it, I don't have the dps to kill it in time, even with the strongest ship of the class I'm allowed to bring in this mission.

There might be a way to cheese through this, but with the 10 minutes at the start to waste my time, it's just not worth trying. The only reason I got this far was the sunk cost fallacy.

The game has great concept. I like first half of the game, it is exactly what I was looking for. Combat is amazing, missions are nice and later wars against factions are great fun. Ship mode graphics are very crisp. I like the style, although it is clearly product of a small budget. 

Up to this point, it is great game, challenging, but fun. Sure, it crashes every 2 hours randomly, but whatever. I can live with that. 

But at the mid or end of the main story, it is clear that the developer had little to no resources for actually finishing, polishing and balancing the game. I get it. I bought the game at full price for 9 euro, which means he gets maybe 5. And I suspect majority of purchases are during sales, which makes his revenue (not profit) in range 1-2 euro per copy. I pity him for this, he deserves more money for such great game, but it is what it is. 

I think the main problem is there are too many systems that he could not possibly balance or even deprecate as non-functional concept. And this is my main problem. 

For instance the overworld combat. I have no idea about how it is implemented internally, but from what I experienced there is insane discrepancy between ship combat and overworld combat. At least when fighting Outsiders - the endgame faction. 

There are main story missions where you need to destroy Outsider fleet with yours of maybe 1.5x size of the enemy's. You have a destroyer, they have a destroyer. And you win quite easily. It is challenging, sure, it may take few attempts before you realize their weapons are strong, but you win with 2/3 or 1/2 of your fleet left. 

But when fights are conducted in overworld mode, you will just lose even with bigger fleet. And I am not talking like 2x size fleet. I understand that enemy ships are stronger. But when they have 30 ships, where only 1 is a destroyer, their fleet should be obliterated against your 30 destroyers, 40 frigates and 50 corvettes. Just because the amount of time and resources to acquire this fleet is considerably higher. 

And with this you fully arrive to non-balanced semi-finished part of the game. These overworld results are not consistent for some reason. Because sometimes you just win with very little casualities. I have no idea why, it may very well be a bug.

So sure, then you say "ok, lets bruteforce it" and you will just sit in your base and keep spamming ships and watching the other factions to lose horribly against Outsiders. Then you face the issue of UI that is well-polished for first part of the game (it is quite immersive), but is very annoying in lategame, when you play the game more like an RTS. 

But maybe it is intended. Maybe at this point such a game is lost strategically and I should start playing from scratch. But I think it is just lack of game polish and balance in lategame area. Understandable due to above reasons, but it's annoying nevertheless.

Is this the definitive 4X and Dogfight combination space game? Not quite. But for 8 Euros its a fun game to sink a few hours into.

The Ships control well, and especially flying smaller craft is fun - dodging around larger ship's firing arcs to get into range. Larger ships move lumberingly, as you would expect, and i can see how some players would prefer piloting a slow but powerful ship instead as well. Overall, having played a bunch of similar games, i'm impressed at how intuitive and 'correct' flying a ship in VD2 feels compared to those other titles.

I really like the way the ships and stations look in game, as well as the bullets and missiles. In larger engagements, it can get a little crowded of course, but i don't see a way around that either. I've seen other reviews critisising the look of the game though, so i guess the graphics are very subjective.

Just based on those two things alone, this game is worth giving a try. The best part of this game IMO is flying around with a small group of smaller ships, and if that's all you're looking for, here you go!


Other than that however....

The quests are passable. Some are better than others, but mostly it comes down to 'fly here, destroy this', which isn't revolutionary, but, well, passable. The story is similar. Some small amount of exploration, but mostly 'fly here, fight this fleet'. The issue here is that there is no real indication of how difficult the encounters are before you start them - and taking the 'recommended' amount of ships will usually leave you way outgunned.
The solution here is to always be over-prepared, and to amass one massive fleet to steamroll every story quest, which leads to the next issue: Crashes and Lags.

The game auto-saves very often, which at least allows you to get back to the crash point quickly, but considering a main draw of the game is getting a large fleet together, that part is very very unstable. Some ship types are especially prone to crashing the game, which can lead to repeating the same fight several times to try and get lucky.

The fleet portion of the game generally feels a little underdeveloped. Controlling fleets remotely works alright, but for some reason cant be done everywhere, requiring you to dock somewhere first. Managing ship types in fleets is a massive pain, and managing stations is even worse. Its a shame then that the chaos in large battles as well as the crashing incentivises using these mechanics more and more as the game goes on. The UI is generally not great either.

Even so, give it a try - I still feel like the flight sim alone is worth the price of admission, and if you can stand the rest, that's just bonus on top.

This game is Amazing. As it is, its a bunch of 4X systems mashed together with a mount and blade over world style of map movement. Main difference is that time does not stop when not on the overworld, allowing for fleets to reinforce you or your enemy (my favorite feature BTW). 

It has many rough edges and could do with a lot of polish but its like 4 years old now so that's not happening. Which is a shame, this game has the potential to be something truly special and i think would have been much better received if it had gotten a little more attention to the user experience. 

The one man dev here is freakishly talented as i have not seen ship AI perform anywhere near as good as it does in this game. I mean games like star citizen and X4 ship AI do not come close to purforming as inteligently as ships do here. Not to say that it competes with Human but you cant win dog fights solo without exploiting the auto targeting of the enemys weapons (and it almost seems like they can do the same to you at times), and constently changing your venctors of movement. 

All in all, it is a fantastic game worth every cent of the 10 dollars it costs.

Ok, so I recommend it, but just barely.
First, I want to mention that playing Void Destroyer 1 is absolutely not required. In fact, I tried it and couldn't bare with the controls so I quit within a couple of hours. In contrast, it's amazing how a few tweaks to the control made a world of difference and thus I was hooked to VD2.

And the beginning is quite solid. The first stage of the game in which you pilot a single ship, do a mix of scripted and and non-scripted missions and progress towards bigger ships. Some cracks begin to appear, though. The scripted missions have horrible balance and obscure winning conditions. Without too much spoiler, there is a ship you're supposed to protect and the mission will fail if it dies, but it is scripted to die and you will succeed the mission if you hit another hidden criteria.

Another balance issue I found which at first sounds like a feature, but is really a must: there is an option to "tweak the difficulty" by reducing the amount of damage your main ship takes. Turns out the missions are so lopsided that I found the game unplayable unless I increased it to its maximum level. And even then, I almost never completed a mission on my first try.

Then the game transitions from a first person ship pilot to a 3rd person fleet manager. The concept is amazing, but the execution pretty bad. I say bad, not horrible, because I have a hard time accomplishing anything I want to do, but it's not flat out impossible.

At least every ship in my fleet and every base have a high level of autonomy. And again, while it might seem like a feature, it becomes a failure because I don't know what's going on. 

Which is a recurring  theme. There are way too many systems which conceptually are awesome, but the execution is obscure. And I read the guide, mind you. For instance, bases are largely automated, but there are a few player controlled options like if it should buy are sell some resources. Despite this, I have no idea of the impact changing any of these settings do.

In a similar fashion, I had to read a guide on how to make money because I needed 11M to buy the required ship whereas missions only paied in Ks. That's when I learned the importance of trade ships. I was soon flooded with money... until they started to blow up faster than I could replace them. So I started to give them escorts... Until the endgame faction started to appear and there ridiculously overpowered ships obliterated whatever escort I would give. It came to the point where the UPKEEP alone of my escort was HIGHER than the income from the trade ship, and I WOULD STILL LOSE THE CONVOY!!!!

And that was the final nail in the coffin for me.

TL;DR : lots of cool concept poorly executed; fun early game, horrible end game.

- It says the default FOV is 120. I turned it up to 150 and still felt like 50.

>> Ships waddling around.
- Their rotation has a huge drag in comparison to their strife (side-to-side movement) speed. In combat, it results in a lot of struggle pulling back the rotation momentum of your ship while your target (and yourself if you're dodging bullets) keep zipping about faster than the rotation control can keep up. (These ships can circle around you faster than your ship can turn in full circle.)
Then for some reason, the default mouse control option is in an auto-center mode, meaning I have to keep pushing my mouse one direction if I'm circling in a dogfight. Not sure why this option is even considered when all it does is fighting the control / making the sense of rotation inconsistent (on top of the rotation drag). I hate that it is a default setting. I hate that I had to find it to turn it off.
- Leading shots, its HUD target guide, its auto-aim, or turrets are incredible unreliable because of how fast these ships can strife / change trajectory in comparison to how quickly & accurately you can aim due to the rotation drag.
The only mostly-reliable weapon was the first very basic ship's laser cannon and sling-shotting my ship's rotation to vaguely aim at my targets directly.
I upgraded the ship into a medium fighter class, which has more guns and health, to see if it fixes some other jitters and combat balancing issues. But it has weaker laser, moves slower (more rotation drag), and now I'm a larger target. The camera still jitters. So those little hostile ships loaded with turrets (because they obviously can't be bothered to turn and aim like I have to) circles around and spray-and-pray all they want and it's harder to dodge and fight back than when I was piloting the basic beginner ship.
Why would I keep grind to upgrade when it made the experience even worse?
- it's hard to see what I'm fighting most of the time. My enemies felt more arbitrary than personal, hard to feel anything other than getting annoyed by my own ship's controls.
- The ship keeps moving forward on its on by default. I have to manually Shift+S to make it stop. And I have to do that every time I completed a travel or came out of a dock. 
Similar to that auto-centering mouse cursor, all it does is adding another unnecessary management and causing inconsistent orientation in combat.

>> Weak situational feedback
- There are a lot of visual inputs happening by default, more than it needs in my opinion (such as showing my ship's health in 2 different ways in on e screen, or some bars jittering 4 different directions depending on how my ship is moving, which jitters all the time).
Then when something hits, a faint red glow to that direction and a tiny ball of fire that disappears after a frame, no audible sound since everything sounds muffled.
It's an important feedback. And space may be void of audible sound, but my ship should still sound like a car crash to a pilot sitting in it when it's about to blow up.
It's hard to notice these and I have to keep looking at the health number thingy to decide whether or not I'm going to pursue my target or spin around.

Clunky in so many ways.

This is a game with a few different layers. You can fly an individual ship, aiming and shooting and such. You can bring AI ships with you, and command them in a tactical interface. And you can control fleets like individual units on a world map. The latter is also how you do long-distance travel with your own ship or fleet, with accelerated time.

None of these work well.

In the early game, when flying your own ship is at its most relevant, you're flying this twitchy thing against other twitchy things. I am not some dogfighting pro, but I've played other space dogfighting games before, like Descent Freespace, and it should not be that hard just to hit something. Later on this gets better when the ships slow down, but by then it's just not that relevant anymore.

Tactical mode is by far the worst part of the game. The camera controls are just utterly bizarre, and you can't even see anything until you toggle on faction outlines, which you'll have to do every time you enter tactical mode. If you do manage to give orders to your ships, often they seem to just fail to execute them. And ships can have active abilities, but they will never use them on their own. It's very awkward activating them yourself for all, say, 35 ships you brought. The game does not help you much here.

The world map mode is passable, but when things are close together (which is very common), it becomes hard, and often outright impossible, to click the thing you meant to click. There is some trade concept but it's overly simplistic and overpowered. Then to balance how easy money it is, the creator put in some weird, unintuitive limitations, like just not being allowed to put more than one trade ship in a fleet other than the one you're personally flying in.

In general, the UI across the entire game requires way too many clicks and mode transitions. For example, say you are in a station and you want to check your faction relationships. Faction information is only available in the world map, so you have to leave the station (plays an animation), and then enter the world map (takes a few seconds) just to check that.

I also experienced frequent crashes, but I never lost much progress because of them, because they were always immediately after an autosave or when leaving a station.

After a while, I realized this game has a lot in common with Mount & Blade, with its living world, its world map, and its action encounters. I do enjoy that formula, and I managed to have some fun with this game, in spite of all its flaws. But I hope to one day see this type of game where most of the parts actually work.

TLDR: X4 lite, does some things better, but some worse, Mount & Blade Warband in space, but needs some QoL improvements & fixes. It's more of an RTS/RT4X and bit less of a management sim than X4.

Long version:

Initially I did not want to purchase it because of the cartoony graphics, but you stop noticing that after a while. If that is the only reason you're not buying it, just buy the game. I'm really loving it.

The game is not as complex as X4:Foundations but not as arcadey as Starpoint Gemini:Warlords either. 

Like other people said it is similar to Mount&Blade in space, perhaps the map is even more similar to Sea Dogs. You travel around in an overworld, but unlike in MnB, you can zoom back in at any spot and all units exist in both the overworld and the 3D world in the same location (the fleets, not individual units). But unlike in X4, you cannot use the fast travel in first person.

I like that it has many different ship classes and almost all the modern/sci-fi "rates": fighters, gunships, corvettes, frigates, destroyers, cruisers (eat that X4), carriers and battleships (called dreadnaughts), and utility vessels. Most of these are available in light, medium and heavy versions.

The tactical control screen is really useful during battles. Battles themselves feel alot more controllable than in X4. making it a decent mix between RTS and space shooter. 

Another cool thing is ships cost money to operate: u can't just have a giant (active) fleet without a large income (through bounties, trading ships or bases making money). 

I doubt I'll play this for the nearly 1000 hours I played X3TC and the few hundred hours I played X4, maybe at most 200 or 300 hours, but that's not necessarily a bad thing: progress is faster, meaning u spend less time grinding imaginary money.

Spoiler/hint: don't try to make the initial money by grinding missions, start trading as soon as you can afford a small transport and the next fighter up from the starter ship. That way your trade ship has 2 escorts. I spent too much time grinding bounties/missions before trading.

While I do like the game, there are some negative aspects as well:
- Crashes every hour or every 2 hours. Luckily it happens mostly just after the game is autosaved, during transitions to bases and battles.
- Some controls are a bit wonky or don't always work if u click too fast.
- Needs quality of life improvements, removing units from groups (tactical view), easier combing and separating of fleets, and ability to just remove your own ship from a fleet in an easier way.
(edit: having a carrier makes that somewhat easier, also the carrier allows u to separate yourself from your fleet alot more easily, kinda silly that with other ships it's more tedious)
- Ability to deselect units from the list on the right bottom in tactical view would be useful
- Shield points are not visible in tactical mode, meaning you have to switch to each ship individually to see shield points, to know if they need shield replenish activated or not.
- AI doesn't use secondary weapons, at least not that I noticed.
- The camera makes weird jumps when entering tactical view and focusing on units too often.
- Waypoint traders seem to reset everytime I load a game.

There are also some things that are both good and bad:

- Slowing down of time and controlling every unit is good and bad:

Rough around the edges with several issues, 4/10
Attempting to be a game like the X series or star citizen. But with a heavier focus on fleet combat/control, which sadly don't work so well.

Art: it has a quite unique artstyle I do like, the toony look might not be for everybody but it does make it look unique. Ships mix bag, I personally like the Skyhawk and the Drake, but there are also quite boxy ones like the gremlin that are… special.

Ship Controls: at first it was getting a bit used to but once I did it was fine, nothing to add or gripe about. (except maybe the high skill ceiling for time control but that’s just me being an idiot)

Tactical/Map Controls: Scrolling is either very slow or super fast, you could try to scroll out just a bit and suddenly you’re looking at ants, or in and you can read the license number on the ship parts, Panning has the same problems and the camera has the tendency to snap to a random location either between the ship and the target or just the ship, which can be annoying if your trying to setup orders.

Gameplay: It starts like any typical space game, small dingy ship you want to replace asap, doing some low level quests to get some cash to tech up. 
Being slightly repetitive with quests having no middle of the road level, it's either ace fighter pilot or babies first fight until you are able to bring your own fleet but then the game also loves boxing you in, giving the option of hiring ships to assist you up to a max of 5 which helps you with some of the quests but randomly just not joining in or the quest specifically states your not allowed to bring allies but still tosses you in an angry beehive of ships equal or higher class of what your allowed to bring, and punching up weight is a one way street.
Ships are very limited in upgrades which for me just makes the standard armor/shield upgrades and missiles/self repair for actives.

Bugs/Glitches: luckily I haven’t run into game breaking bugs, (as far as I’m aware) but there are plenty of bugs/glitches that can be annoying. Besides the Map one, there have been a few, like the revenge mission occasionally doesn’t spawn the enemies until you leave and enter a few times, which funnily enough you can use to cycle between enemies if they do spawn.
Your scroll wheel affects your second screen if you pan to far over to it, you can bring your mouse back by panning the opposite way, but it's still annoying.
Time compression occasionally turns on as you exit a jump.
After cutscenes you can randomly get put into a third person view.
Sometimes the weapon range markers highlight besides being way out of range or no aim reticle appears besides being in range.
AI for some reason don’t aim up or down unless you’re not watching.


Owned craft seem to fight to the death, as far as I can tell the button which says: “Retreat to allied gate/base” doesn’t do anything. I’m aware of the 10km minimum range for the jump so I have sent ships away, double checked they were 10km out of range of anybody but they would still not flee the battlefield.
Player Ship weapons are just pea shooters, so far I have only found the Reaper and Pilar having a direct upgrade in damage by adding a second half to their turrets but that only helps them against the smaller ships, I regret buying the Drake, but as it took all my money and I haven’t gotten enough to get the anubis or found other frigates to buy so I have no measurement besides the AI which melt the Drake like it's nothing. My main and only damage source against anything bigger than gunships seems to be the missiles which feels cheap.

Conclusion; There is a solid base that make it unique enough from its counterparts, the art style is great, and it does the fleet combat much better than X4 but sadly there are just a lot of problems that make it hard for me to enjoy it over X4.

The endgame for the campaign is what kills it for me, at a certain point a switch is flipped, and the difficulty just relentlessly ramps up without giving a chance to recover, because you're on a time limit of draining resources at that point in time.
The smallcraft combat is decently fun, small scale fleet management fine, and even managing overworld trade isn't half bad, but even with these:
Smallcraft rapidly drop off with the introduction of beams and railguns to several ships' armaments, you can't dodge hitscan unless the AI intentionally misses, and beams actually sting quite badly, especially if you get focused by several.
At larger scales, you have to use active abilities with ships one at a time, which gets incredibly tedious, incredibly fast, doubly so when you either have to look through a list, or select each individual ship in a dogfight, and on a scale of almost a hundred ships on your side, let alone anything that a carrier style ship may launch, let ALONE whatever the enemy fields (Which can commonly outnumber your forces), it's too easy to miss over ships, (And not using them will lead to you getting run over in later story missions).
And the overworld map largely turns into tedium when micromanaging fleet on fleet actions, again the trade menu's good though.

I should not be expected to destroy a nearly equally sized fleet of spoiler story enemies (Boasting power greater than anything the player can ever get stock), with more ships of a larger class than I can field in the particular mission (Estimated 7-8 frigates, where I'm only allowed to field 5), let alone the fact that their ships seem to both be specifically designed to kill capital ships, while also having their main firepower be beams so they can hit smallcraft with ease, and the only reason I won that one was because I cheesed the hell out of them by forcing them to lock onto one ship, then running that ship away so they focused on it and no other craft.
Not to mention it seems like the game demands that you throw ships into a meatgrinder of sheer raw attrition, being expected to replace them after combat every single time, and not bringing these ships are not an option since some missions have what boils down to a DPS check.

The game peaked for me when I got the basebuilding and capture options available, then rapidly dropped off the moment the spoiler story enemies started appearing on the map due to aforementioned constant resource drain pressuring me to rush the storyline, even if it didn't explicitly say to do so.
